bridalPage.title: Bridal mehndi
bridalPage.intro: A trial first, then the evening itself, at home or at the venue.

photo.alt: A bride in a red lehenga by a tall window, turned away, her face in shadow

bridalPage.trial:
An hour at the studio, about six weeks before. We try two or three patterns on one hand, check your skin, and talk through how far it goes and anything you'd like hidden in it.

The trial is included with hands to the elbow, and taken off the price of any bridal package booked within a month.
before: Nails, waxing and any scrub the day before: nothing on the skin after the henna.
Clean, dry hands and feet. No cream or oil.
Eat first, and have someone ready to feed you.
A table, a chair with a back, good light, and somewhere quiet for four to six hours.
bridalPage.travel:
We come to you anywhere within the M25 at no charge. Further afield, we add travel at cost; ask with your postcode.

For weddings abroad, we quote travel and stay with the bridal package.

questions.q: How far ahead should I book?
questions.a: Summer Saturdays go about a year ahead. Weekdays and winter weddings, often a few months. Check your date on the home page.

questions.q: How long does bridal mehndi take?
questions.a: About four hours to the wrist and six to the elbow; feet add two.

questions.q: When should I have it done?
questions.a: Two days before the wedding, in the evening, so it's darkest on the day.

questions.q: Do you travel to the venue?
questions.a: Yes. Anywhere within the M25 at no charge; further, travel at cost.
Yes: henna leaf, lemon and essential oils. We never use black henna.
That's how henna starts. It deepens to brown over about two days; keep it warm and dry.

questions.q: I have sensitive skin. Can I test it?
questions.a: Yes. Ask for a small patch at your trial, or at the studio a week before.

questions.q: How many guests can you do in an evening?
questions.a: One artist does about eighteen floral trails in three hours. We bring up to four artists.
A deposit holds the date; the balance is due a week before. We send the terms with the quote.

pages.title: Natural henna,|and a patch test
pages.description: What's in Hatheli's henna paste, why it starts orange, and patch tests for sensitive skin.
pages.intro: Leaf, lemon and oil. Nothing that stains black.

blocks.heading: The paste
blocks.body:
Powdered henna leaf, fresh lemon juice, sugar and a little lavender and tea tree oil. Mixed each week and kept frozen until the morning it's used.

No PPD, no chemical darkeners, nothing that stains black in an hour.

blocks.heading: A patch test
blocks.body: If your skin reacts easily, or it's your first time, ask for a small patch at your trial. We'll put a single motif on the inside of your wrist and you'll see it develop over two days.

blocks.heading: Black henna
blocks.body: We never use it. What the NHS says about it, and the day we last checked, is on our aftercare page.

pages.title: Getting the|darkest stain
pages.description: Why henna starts orange and what helps it darken, from Hatheli's artists.
pages.intro: Most of it happens after we leave.

blocks.heading: Time
blocks.body: Henna stains the top layer of skin and keeps darkening for two days. The longer the paste stays on, the deeper it goes.

blocks.heading: Warmth
blocks.body: Warm hands stain darker. A cup of tea, a warm room, gloves for bed.

blocks.heading: Water
blocks.body: Keep it away until the morning after. Then wash as normal.

pages.title: Mehndi styles,|explained
pages.description: Traditional, Arabic, Indo-Arabic and contemporary mehndi, and what each one suits.
pages.intro: Four ways to draw on a hand.

blocks.heading: Traditional
blocks.body: Dense, covering the hand, with figures, peacocks and the bride and groom. The longest to do.

blocks.heading: Arabic
blocks.body: Bold trails with skin left bare between them. Quick, and striking from across a room.

blocks.heading: Indo-Arabic
blocks.body: The two together: fine fill inside bold outlines.

blocks.heading: Contemporary
blocks.body: Fine lines, a lot of skin, often one finger or the back of the hand.
